The bow that carries the string is a flexible wooden member about 125 to 135 cm long overall. The resonator is a gourd, and a thin wooden stick and an inzebe rattle are also used; two rings on the string draw the bow closer together, and a third ring is tied by a cord to the gourd resonator. Cloth or banana peel is laid between the bow and the resonator so that they do not touch directly. The source does not state the materials of the rings and the cord.

It is made by the Twa and used by the Hutu, and it came into Rwanda together with the ikembe at the beginning of the twentieth century. Besides the traditional plant-fibre and animal-gut strings, metal strings have become widely used. The instrument is played at festivals and official ceremonies and also appears in the ikinimba dance, which tells the stories of Rwandan kings and heroes; it can be played solo without accompaniment and is used in many kinds of music.

The umuduri is a chordophone of Burundi and Rwanda, H-S number 311.111, of the bow-shaped kind. It carries its string on a flexible wooden bow with a gourd attached as a resonator, and it is played together with a wooden stick and an inzebe rattle. The player holds the bow vertically in front of the body with the left hand and presses the gourd against the body, while the right hand strikes the string with a thin stick and holds the inzebe rattle; the string is divided into two unequal lengths that give two basic notes, and the fingers then shorten the longer segment to obtain a third. This instrument is made by the Twa and used by the Hutu, and it appears commonly at festivals and official ceremonies, for instance accompanying the ikinimba dance; it can also be played alone and is used in many kinds of music.
烏姆杜里琴擁有溫潤而內斂的音色，帶有淡淡的蒼涼感。其聲音質地柔和卻富有穿透力，音: The umuduri has a warm, inward timbre with a faint air of desolation. Its sound is soft in texture yet carries well, and its range runs from the middle-low to the middle-high register, so it can show delicate expression. It resonates in a distinctive way: the vibrating string interacts with the wooden bearer, producing a warm resonant foundation, and the timbre changes greatly with playing technique. Compared with the bright clarity of the guitar, the umuduri sounds more mysterious and reserved; compared with the violin, its sound is rawer and coarser, with the weathered flavour of a folk tradition. The traditional gut string gives the instrument a warm, full tone, while the modern metal string adds brightness and penetration, giving the timbre more expressive tension.
